# formatting: a real minus sign, fixed decimals

  s <- formatC(abs(x), format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
  ifelse(x < 0, paste0("−", s), s)
}
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(num(x, d), "%")
out <- function(id, col = "value") outputs[[col]][outputs$output_id == id]

## Introduction

::: {.report-intro}
![](assets/opa/opa-details.png){.opa-figure}

This report rebuilds, step by step, the RJKDC side's fiscal score of California's
Proposition 40 (the Billionaire Tax Act): a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires
resident in California on 1 January 2026. The authors argue that the tax would collect far less
than its proponents expect, and that billionaires who leave take their income tax with them for
ever, so the state ends up poorer. Following the
[Open Policy Analysis](https://tinyurl.com/1qypbihb) framework:

- **Open Output**: [the explorer](explorer/), the mean net present value and share of
  negative outcomes for every combination of seven inputs
- **Open Analysis**: this document, and [the slide deck](slides/slides.html)
- **Open Materials**: [the materials page](materials.html), every script, test, CSV and
  source, with all nine mismatches found along the way
:::

**What is reproduced.** Two versions of one analysis, side by side, as fixed in the project's
pre-specified output before any results were seen:

1. **SSRN 6340778** (Rauh, Jaros, Kearney, Doran and Cosso, Hoover Institution, 17 March 2026).
   Headline: revenue of about \$`r h("ssrn","revenue_headline","printed")`B and a mean NPV of
   `r num(h("ssrn","mc_mean_npv","printed"))` \$B, with `r h("ssrn","mc_pct_negative","printed")`%
   of simulated outcomes negative (PDF p.1).
2. **NBER chapter c15504** (Jaros and Rauh, 22 September 2026), the litigation-weighted revision.
   Headline: revenue of about \$30B (\$`r h("nber","revenue_range_low","printed")`B to
   \$`r h("nber","revenue_range_high","printed")`B) and a mean NPV of
   `r num(h("nber","mc_mean_npv","printed"))` \$B, with `r h("nber","mc_pct_negative","printed")`%
   negative.

Both are reproduced from the authors' own public, MIT-licensed code and data
([github.com/bjaros20/wealth_tax](https://github.com/bjaros20/wealth_tax), pinned at commit
`25e84dd`): their Excel workbooks are read cell by cell, their R scripts are ported line by line
and also re-run unmodified, and the NBER person-level file `final.csv` is summed directly. Every
number in this document is read from the project's `{targets}` pipeline at render time; the only
numbers typed in are the papers' printed values we compare against, each with its PDF page
(page numbers are PDF pages throughout).

**The shape of the argument**, in one line: net present value = wealth tax collected once, minus
the present value of the income tax that departing billionaires would have paid in every future
year. Sections 4 and 5.1 of the paper estimate the two pieces; Sections 5.2 to 5.5 combine them.
We follow that order, then list what the NBER revision changes.

### Notation, in one place

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| $\tau$ | statutory wealth tax rate | share |
| $WT$ | one-time wealth tax revenue actually collected | \$B |
| $C$ | annual California income tax paid by the billionaires | \$B per year |
| $f$ | share of that income tax base that leaves the state | share |
| $r$ | real discount rate (the Monte Carlo's draw) | per year |
| $g$ | real growth of the lost income tax stream | per year |
| $\varepsilon$ | migration semi-elasticity: % of the base lost per percentage point of tax | |
| $q$ | probability the Act survives constitutional challenge (NBER only) | probability |
| NPV | $WT - f \cdot C/r$ (or $/(r-g)$), the net fiscal effect today | \$B |

## Section 4: the wealth tax revenue

### 4.1 The baseline, before anyone leaves (eq. 3)

$$R_{\text{baseline}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \tau \times \text{TaxBase}_i$$

In words: take each of the $N$ = `r inp("n_billionaires")` California billionaires on the 2025
Forbes list (with the authors' corrections), subtract their directly held residential real estate
(the Act exempts it), multiply what is left by the `r pct(100*inp("tax_rate"),0)` rate, and add up.
Their aggregate net worth is \$`r num(inp("baseline_net_worth"))`B. The workbook's own row-by-row
sum gives **\$`r num(rc$baseline_precise, 2)`B**; the paper prints \$94.20B (p.10). The
difference is [mismatch 6](materials.html#mismatches): the paper's text rounds the workbook's
cell, and every later step then uses the typed literal `r rc$baseline_literal` rather than the
workbook's own sum. We reproduce the code, so later steps use `r rc$baseline_literal` too.

### 4.2 The six confirmed departures (eq. 4, 6 to 8)

$$R_{\text{adjusted}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (1 - \text{Departed}_i) \times \tau \times \text{TaxBase}_i$$

The same sum, dropping anyone publicly reported to have moved out before the 1 January 2026
residency date: Page, Brin, Thiel, Hankey, Spielberg and Sacks (Table 6, p.11). Revenue falls to
**\$`r num(rc$confirmed6_ceiling, 2)`B** (printed: \$`r out("revenue_confirmed6","printed_value")`B).
The paper then asks how big a behavioural response that is. It divides the share of revenue lost
by the rate change, in percentage points (eq. 5):

$$\varepsilon = \frac{\%\Delta \text{TaxBase}}{\Delta \text{TaxRate (p.p.)}}
 = \frac{(94.20 - 67.51)/94.20}{5} = 5.67$$

```{r}
#| label: semi-elasticity
#| code-summary: "the implied semi-elasticities, recomputed"
eps6  <- 100 * (1 - rc$confirmed6_ceiling / rc$baseline_literal) / (100 * inp("tax_rate"))
eps10 <- 100 * (1 - rc$expanded10_estimate / rc$baseline_literal) / (100 * inp("tax_rate"))
c(confirmed_6 = eps6, expanded_10 = eps10)
```

A semi-elasticity of `r num(eps6, 2)` means that a 1-point tax rate rise drives out about
`r num(eps6, 1)`% of the base. The authors treat this as a floor because it counts only departures
that made the news.

### 4.3 The expanded departures (eq. 9 to 11)

Adding four more reported or rumoured leavers (Zuckerberg after the snapshot date; Koum, Hastings
and Fang unconfirmed; Table 7, p.12), revenue falls to **\$`r num(rc$expanded10_estimate, 2)`B**
(printed \$`r out("revenue_expanded10","printed_value")`B), and the implied semi-elasticity rises
to `r num(eps10, 2)`. The paper argues that people who left after the snapshot date may still escape
the tax, because the retroactive residency date may not survive in court (pp.12-13).

### 4.4 The literature calibration (eq. 12 to 14)

$$\varepsilon_{\text{lit}} = 0.24 \times 43.00 = 10.32, \qquad
R^{\text{lit}} = (1 - \varepsilon_{\text{lit}} \times 0.05) \times 94.20$$

Brülhart et al. (2022) estimate that Swiss taxable wealth falls by 43% per point of wealth tax,
about 24% of it through people moving. The authors keep only the moving part,
`r inp("brulhart_semi_elasticity")`, and apply it linearly to the full 5-point rate: the base shrinks
by `r pct(100 * rc$migration_share)` and revenue is **\$`r num(rc$literature_calibrated, 2)`B**
(printed \$`r out("revenue_literature_calibrated","printed_value")`B). Two things to notice. First,
that is a Swiss estimate for a recurring annual tax, applied here to a one-time tax; the paper
argues a one-time tax with easy interstate moves could provoke a *larger* response (p.14), and the
BSZ side disputes exactly this ([disputes row 1](https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40/blob/main/comparison/DISPUTES.md)).
Second, a linear 10.32 × 5 = 51.6% loss is steeper than the log form the NBER revision later uses
(41.1%, NBER PDF p.23).

### 4.5 The preferred revenue estimate

The paper settles on "approximately \$`r h("ssrn","revenue_headline","printed")` billion (range:
\$35-46 billion)" (p.14). The top of the range is the literature calibration, \$`r num(rc$literature_calibrated, 2)`B.
The bottom comes from a judgement that the true semi-elasticity is 12 to 13 (footnote 6, p.14),
which the authors call "plausible and conservative". The \$40B point itself is not computed
anywhere in the authors' code; it sits near the middle of that range. **Labelled guesswork**
in this reproduction.

## Section 5.1: the income tax the billionaires pay

### The Pareto upper bound (eq. 15 and 16)

$$N(y) = A\,y^{-\alpha}, \qquad S(k, n) = \left(\frac{k}{n}\right)^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}$$

The state publishes how many tax returns report income above \$1M, \$2M, \$3M, \$4M, \$5M and
\$10M (FTB PIT Annual Report 2024, Table B-4A). If top incomes follow a Pareto distribution, the log
of those counts falls on a straight line against the log of the thresholds, with slope $-\alpha$.
The fitted line gives $\hat\alpha$ = **`r num(pf$alpha, 3)`** (printed `r out("pareto_alpha","printed_value")`,
$R^2$ = `r num(pf$r_squared, 4)`).

```{r}
#| label: f-pareto
#| fig-cap: "The six published filer counts against their AGI thresholds, log-log, with the fitted Pareto line (paper Figure 1)."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.6
d <- data.frame(y = pf$thresholds, n = pf$filer_counts)
ggplot(d, aes(y, n)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = log10(pf$A), slope = -pf$alpha, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "#1f6fce") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "AGI threshold", y = "Returns above the threshold") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

$S(k, n)$ is the share of the bracket's income that goes to its top $k$ of $n$ filers. With the
top `r inp("n_billionaires")` of the 4,729 filers above \$10M, the continuous formula gives
`r pct(100 * sch$continuous_top_share)` of the bracket's \$`r inp("bracket_tax_ty23")`B of tax.
The script then builds a rank-by-rank income schedule and rescales it by
`r num(sch$rescale_factor, 3)` so that its top 212 match the continuous share (footnote 12: the
discrete sum undershoots by about 11%). Scaling Tax Year 2023 to FY 2024-25 collections
(\$`r inp("total_pit_fy25")`B in total) multiplies by `r num(attr(itmc, "scale_factor"), 3)`. If
the billionaires *are* the 212 highest earners, they pay **\$`r num(t8$mean_fy25[t8$K == 212], 2)`B
a year**. That is the upper bound, and the top of $C$'s range.

### The dispersion Monte Carlo (Table 8)

Billionaires are ranked by wealth, not income, and many realise little income in a given year. So
the script places the 212 billionaires at random among the top $K$ filers (without replacement,
100,000 draws for each $K$ from 212 to 2,000) and sums their tax. The wider the pool, the lower the
expected total. The authors take $K \approx 500$ ("roughly the top decile of the bracket") as a
reasonable floor, which gives the bottom of $C$'s range, \$3.3B. The choice of $K$ = 500 is a
judgement, not an estimate, so the range $C \in [3.3, 5.8]$ is labelled **guesswork** below.

```{r}
#| label: t-table8
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "Table 8: reproduced (seed 42, the authors' RNG stream replayed) vs printed"
p8 <- printed[printed$table == "table8", ]
pv <- function(k, col) p8$printed[p8$row == k & p8$column == col]
tab8 <- t8 %>% transmute(
  `Pool size K` = format(K, big.mark = ","),
  `Mean` = num(mean_fy25, 3), `printed` = sapply(K, pv, "mean"),
  `P5` = num(p05_fy25, 3), `printed ` = sapply(K, pv, "p05"),
  `P95` = num(p95_fy25, 3), `printed  ` = sapply(K, pv, "p95"))
m8 <- sum(round(t8$mean_fy25, 2) == sapply(t8$K, pv, "mean")) +
      sum(round(t8$p05_fy25, 2) == sapply(t8$K, pv, "p05")) +
      sum(round(t8$p95_fy25, 2) == sapply(t8$K, pv, "p95"))
scroll(kable(tab8, align = "rrrrrrr", caption = "Table 8, $B per year (PDF p.17)"))
```

`r m8` of the `r 3 * nrow(t8)` cells round to the printed value; the tests hold this at the printed rounding
(`tests/testthat/test-income-tax-mc.R`).

## Section 5.2: from an annual loss to a present value (eq. 17 to 20)

$$PV = \frac{C}{r}, \qquad NPV = WT - f \cdot \frac{C}{r}$$

$$\text{or, with growth:}\qquad PV = \frac{C}{r - g}, \qquad NPV = WT - f \cdot \frac{C}{r - g}$$

This is the step that makes the result. The wealth tax is collected **once**. The income tax of
anyone who leaves is lost **every year, for ever**, and a perpetuity paying $C$ a year is worth
$C/r$ today. At $r$ = 1.5% a perpetuity is worth 1/0.015, about 67 years of payments; at 4.5%,
about 22. The paper's text then argues the lost stream grows with the billionaires' wealth, making
it a growing perpetuity, $C/(r-g)$, and calibrates $r - g$ at about 1.5% from the S&P 500's
dividend yield (p.18).

Two things are worth knowing before reading the tables:

- **Which rate is drawn.** Tables 9 and 10 label their rates $(r-g)$. The Monte Carlo in Sec 5.5
  draws "$r$" and computes $C/r$. The SSRN code (`NPV_dist.R:60`) divides by the plain draw, and the
  NBER code draws the same interval but calls it $(r-g)$
  ([mismatches 2 and 3](materials.html#mismatches)). Numerically nothing changes, because the same
  interval is used whatever it is called; conceptually, the interval is asked to stand for two
  different things. The explorer's growth dial shows what the ambiguity is worth.
- **The horizon.** Treating the loss as permanent is itself one of the disputed choices: the
  BSZ side scores the loss as lasting about the five payment years
  ([disputes row 2](https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40/blob/main/comparison/DISPUTES.md)).

## Section 5.3: NPV by departure scenario (Table 9)

Three scenarios, each a revenue figure paired with an income tax figure, each at three rates. The
departure share is implied by the revenue: $f = 1 - WT/94.20$, so revenue lost and income tax lost
move together ([disputes row 6](https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40/blob/main/comparison/DISPUTES.md)
questions that proportionality).

```{r}
#| label: t-table9
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "Table 9 from compute_npv_table9() (NPV_calculations_5.2.xlsx ported) vs printed"
p9 <- printed[printed$table == "table9", ]
t9p <- t9 %>% mutate(key = paste0(scenario, "@", r)) %>% rowwise() %>% mutate(
  pv_printed = p9$printed[p9$row == key & p9$column == "pv_lost"],
  npv_printed = p9$printed[p9$row == key & p9$column == "npv"]) %>% ungroup()
tab9 <- t9p %>% transmute(Scenario = label, `WT ($B)` = num(WT, 2), `C ($B)` = num(C, 2),
  `f` = pct(100 * f), `r - g` = pct(100 * r),
  `PV lost` = num(pv_lost), `printed` = num(pv_printed),
  `NPV` = num(npv), `printed ` = num(npv_printed))
m9 <- sum(abs(round(t9p$pv_lost, 1) - t9p$pv_printed) < 1e-9) + sum(abs(round(t9p$npv, 1) - t9p$npv_printed) < 1e-9)
scroll(kable(tab9, align = "lrrrrrrrr", caption = "Table 9, $B (PDF p.19)"))
```

`r m9` of the `r 2 * nrow(t9p)` cells match the printed digit. The central scenario's \$`r inp("wt_central_scenario")`B is a
typed literal with no derivation anywhere ([mismatch 8](materials.html#mismatches)), which is why
the input table labels it **scenario**. Note that the headline \$`r num(h("ssrn","mc_mean_npv","printed"))`B
is *not* a cell of this table: the central cell at 1.5% is
`r num(t9$npv[t9$scenario=="central" & t9$r==0.015])` \$B. The headline is the Monte Carlo mean of Sec 5.5.

## Section 5.4: the break-even departure share (Table 10, eq. 21)

$$x^* = \frac{WT \cdot (r - g)}{C}$$

Set NPV to zero and solve for the departure share: the tax pays for itself only if fewer than
$x^*$ of the income tax base leaves. The script computes $WT \cdot r / C$ with the drawn rate.

```{r}
#| label: t-table10
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "Table 10 from compute_npv_table10() vs printed"
p10 <- printed[printed$table == "table10", ]
tab10 <- t10 %>% mutate(key = paste0(scenario, "@", r)) %>% rowwise() %>%
  mutate(printed = p10$printed[p10$row == key]) %>% ungroup() %>%
  transmute(Scenario = label, `r - g` = pct(100 * r), `x*` = pct(100 * break_even_pct),
            printed = pct(printed))
m10 <- sum(abs(round(100 * t10$break_even_pct, 1) -
  sapply(paste0(t10$scenario, "@", t10$r), function(k) p10$printed[p10$row == k])) < 1e-9)
scroll(kable(tab10, align = "lrrr", caption = "Table 10 (PDF p.20)"))
```

`r m10` of the `r nrow(t10)` cells match. A check that is not an input: plugging each $x^*$ back into the Table 9 formula
must give an NPV of exactly zero (see [internal identities](#internal-identities)).

## Section 5.5: the Monte Carlo behind the headline (eq. 22 to 24)

$$WT \sim U[\$35\text{B}, \$67.1\text{B}], \quad C \sim U[\$3.3\text{B}, \$5.8\text{B}], \quad
r \sim U[0.015, 0.045]$$

$$f = 1 - WT/94.20, \qquad NPV = WT - f\cdot C/r$$

Draw the three inputs independently and uniformly, 100,000 times, and average the NPV. Three
details matter:

1. **The printed upper bound 67.1 is a typo for 67.51** ([mismatch 1](materials.html#mismatches)).
   The code uses `r ss$wt_max`; with 67.1 the printed mean does not come out.
2. **The discount term is $C/r$, not $C/(r-g)$** (mismatch 2), over the whole 1.5% to 4.5% band.
3. **The draw's revenue range is not the preferred revenue.** $WT \sim U[35, 67.51]$ has a mean of
   \$`r num(h("ssrn","mc_expected_revenue"), 2)`B, above the paper's own preferred \$`r h("ssrn","revenue_headline","printed")`B,
   because the ceiling (only the six confirmed departures) enters as the top of the draw.

```{r}
#| label: t-mc
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "Sec 5.5: seeded reproduction vs printed, both versions"
mk <- function(v, lab) {
  s <- if (v == "ssrn") tr("npv_mc_ssrn_summary") else tr("npv_mc_nber_summary")
  data.frame(Version = lab,
    `Mean` = num(s$mean, 2), `printed` = num(h(v, "mc_mean_npv", "printed")),
    `Median` = num(s$median, 2), `printed ` = num(h(v, "mc_median_npv", "printed")),
    `SD` = num(s$sd, 2), `printed  ` = num(h(v, "mc_sd_npv", "printed")),
    `% negative` = num(s$pct_negative, 2), `printed   ` = num(h(v, "mc_pct_negative", "printed")),
    check.names = FALSE)
}
scroll(kable(rbind(mk("ssrn", "SSRN (p.20)"), mk("nber", "NBER (p.35)")),
             align = "lrrrrrrrr", caption = "NPV Monte Carlo, $B, seed 2026, 100,000 draws"))
```

Our R port replays the authors' script exactly (same seed, same draw order) and agrees with an
unmodified run of `NPV_dist.R` to machine precision. The SSRN median and share negative match
the printed values. The mean (`r num(mcs$summary$mean, 2)` against `r num(h("ssrn","mc_mean_npv","printed"))`)
and the standard deviation (`r num(mcs$summary$sd, 2)` against `r h("ssrn","mc_sd_npv","printed")`)
do not quite ([mismatch 9](materials.html#mismatches)). The draws are independent, so the mean has
a closed form:

$$E[NPV] = E[WT] - \left(1 - \frac{E[WT]}{94.20}\right) E[C]\, E\!\left[\tfrac{1}{r}\right]$$

$$E\!\left[\tfrac{1}{r}\right] = \frac{\ln(0.045/0.015)}{0.045 - 0.015}$$

It equals **`r num(tr("npv_mc_ssrn_analytic_mean"), 3)` \$B**, which rounds to the printed
`r num(h("ssrn","mc_mean_npv","printed"))`. So the printed mean is the model's exact expectation,
while the shipped seed gives `r num(mcs$summary$mean, 2)`. The printed SD stays unexplained.

```{r}
#| label: f-npv
#| fig-cap: "The distribution of simulated NPV, both versions (paper Figure 3). Draws below zero in orange; the dashed line is the mean."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
dd <- rbind(data.frame(v = "SSRN, Mar 2026", npv = mcs$draws$npv),
            data.frame(v = "NBER, Sept 2026", npv = mcn$draws$npv))
dd$v <- factor(dd$v, levels = c("SSRN, Mar 2026", "NBER, Sept 2026"))
mm <- dd %>% group_by(v) %>% summarise(m = mean(npv))
ggplot(dd, aes(npv, fill = npv < 0)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(data = mm, aes(xintercept = m), linetype = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#eb6834", `FALSE` = "#1f6fce"), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~v) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-250, 70)) +
  labs(x = "NPV, $B", y = "draws") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## The NBER revision (September 2026)

The NBER version keeps Sections 4 and 5.1 (same base, same Pareto fit, same Table 8, now numbered
Table 9) and changes the revenue side and the Monte Carlo. Five changes, in the order they enter:

1. **A later valuation date.** Net worth is grown 7% to the 31 December 2026 valuation date, and the
   base is rebuilt person by person in `final.csv`: `r nc$n_domestic` domestic rows, face value
   \$`r num(nc$domestic_total_grown, 2)`B (printed \$`r out("nber_domestic_grown","printed_value")`B).
2. **Seven confirmed departures** (the six, plus Travis Kalanick): removing them leaves
   **\$`r num(nc$ceiling_recomputed, 2)`B**. The README says \$72.06B and the script hard-codes 72
   ([mismatch 4](materials.html#mismatches)); three numbers for one quantity. The
   `r nc$n_international` non-US-citizen residents (\$`r num(nc$international_net_worth, 1)`B of net
   worth) stay outside the base, now explicitly.
3. **A litigation discount** (PDF pp.19-23, eqs. 5 to 8). Removing three pre-filing departures
   and Zuckerberg leaves a recognized base of \$`r num(ncol$recognized, 2)`B; multiplying by
   $q$ = `r ncol$q`, the chance the Act survives in court, gives
   $E[R] = q \times R_{\text{recognized}}$ = **\$`r num(ncol$central, 2)`B**
   (printed \$`r h("nber","revenue_headline","printed")`B). Keeping Zuckerberg gives
   \$`r num(ncol$upper, 2)`B; moving the gray-zone names out gives \$`r num(ncol$lower, 2)`B,
   the printed range \$`r h("nber","revenue_range_low","printed")`B to \$`r h("nber","revenue_range_high","printed")`B.
   The choice of $q$ = 0.50 comes from an accounting standard for uncertain tax positions
   (ASC 740-10), not from a legal assessment; it is **guesswork**.
4. **The departure share is drawn on its own**, $f \sim U[`r nb$f_min`, `r nb$f_max`]$,
   independent of revenue, "centered conservatively around the observed wealth-base departure
   fraction" (PDF p.30).
5. **The Monte Carlo draws revenue from zero**: $WT \sim U[0, 72]$ (PDF p.35, eq. 16). Its mean,
   \$`r num(h("nber","mc_expected_revenue"), 0)`B, is $0.5 \times 72$, which the paper calls the
   central estimate (PDF p.33). This is the only place $q$ appears in the code: there is no
   explicit multiplier ([mismatch 5](materials.html#mismatches)), and a uniform draw from 0 is a
   different assumption from a survive-or-not coin flip on a fixed base. The paper also states
   the income tax loss is not scaled by $q$: people who left do not come back if the Act is struck
   down (PDF p.33).

The NBER break-even table, from the same `compute_npv_table10()` at the paper's central
\$36B and \$4.55B:

```{r}
#| label: t-nber-table10
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "NBER Table 10 (PDF p.34): same function, NBER central inputs"
wt36 <- 0.5 * nb$wt_max
n10 <- compute_npv_table10(scenarios = list(central = list(label = "Central", WT = wt36, C = 4.55)))
pn <- printed[printed$table == "nber_table10", ]
scroll(kable(n10 %>% transmute(`WT ($B)` = num(WT, 0), `C ($B)` = num(C, 2), `r - g` = pct(100 * r),
                               `x*` = pct(100 * break_even_pct),
                               printed = pct(pn$printed[match(paste0("central@", r), pn$row)])),
             align = "rrrrr", caption = "NBER Table 10 (PDF p.34)"))
```

The NBER Monte Carlo reproduces its printed summary to within Monte Carlo error with no systematic
gap (table above). Its exact expectation is `r num(tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean"), 2)` \$B, which
rounds to `r num(tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean"), 1)` rather than the printed
`r num(h("nber","mc_mean_npv","printed"))`: here the printed value is the seeded run's, not the
expectation. The explorer shows the exact expectations and says so.

## Every input, by origin {#every-input-by-origin}

This section is not in either paper: it re-sorts every input by *how much evidence stands behind
it*, the question a reader who wants to argue with the result has to answer first.

- **data**: read off a public dataset or the authors' own person-level file, and recomputable from it.
- **research**: an estimate taken from a published paper.
- **guesswork**: set by assumption. Some are bounded by evidence, but no dataset or estimate pins
  the value itself.
- **scenario**: a choice about which policy or counterfactual is being scored.
- **derived**: a value another row implies.

```{r}
#| label: origins
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "every input: the pipeline's inputs.csv plus the explorer's seven dials"
dials <- site_dials(rc)
dial_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(dials, function(d) data.frame(
  input = d$key, what = d$label, `value(s)` = paste(d$labels, collapse = "; "),
  origin = d$origin, where = "explorer dial (R/site.R)", check.names = FALSE)))
inp_rows <- data.frame(input = inputs$input_id, what = inputs$description,
  `value(s)` = ifelse(is.na(inputs$value), "1.5% to 4.5%", vapply(inputs$value, function(v) format(signif(v, 6)), "")),
  origin = inputs$label, where = inputs$source, check.names = FALSE)
odf <- rbind(inp_rows, dial_rows)
scroll(kable(odf, caption = "Inputs by origin (export/r/inputs.csv, then the explorer's dials)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: origins-count
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "how many of each kind"
cnt <- as.data.frame(table(factor(odf$origin, levels = c("data", "research", "guesswork", "scenario", "derived"))))
names(cnt) <- c("origin", "rows")
n_guess_dials <- sum(vapply(dials, function(d) d$origin == "guesswork", logical(1)))
scroll(kable(cnt))
```

**The headline:** `r n_guess_dials` of the `r length(dials)` inputs that move the result in the
explorer are guesswork. The one labelled data, the revenue ceiling, rests on a legal judgement
about who counts as having left (disputes row 3). The data and research inputs (the Forbes base,
the FTB brackets, the Pareto fit, the Swiss semi-elasticity) fix the *scale*; whether the NPV is
negative is decided by the guesswork: how wide the revenue draw is, where the income tax range
stops, which rate is used, and whether the lost income tax is permanent.

## What reproduces

```{r}
#| label: mismatch-summary
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "every exported output against its printed value (export/r/outputs.csv)"
o <- outputs %>% transmute(output = output_id, version, reproduced = signif(value, 6),
  printed = printed_value, `abs diff` = signif(abs_diff, 2),
  page = ifelse(is.na(printed_page), "NBER", printed_page))
scroll(kable(o))
```

Every figure reproduces from the authors' own code to within the tolerances in
`tests/testthat/` (printed rounding for deterministic figures, four Monte Carlo standard errors
for simulated ones). The largest gap is `r outputs$output_id[which.max(outputs$abs_diff)]`
(`r num(max(outputs$abs_diff), 2)`), mismatch 9.
`r sum(grepl("^## [0-9]+\\.", readLines("../MISMATCHES.md")))` discrepancies were found between the
papers, their READMEs and their code. We record them rather than fix them:

```{r}
#| label: mismatch-list
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "the nine mismatches, parsed from MISMATCHES.md"
mm_lines <- grep("^## [0-9]+\\.", readLines("../MISMATCHES.md"), value = TRUE)
cat(paste0(sub("^## ", "", mm_lines), collapse = "\n"), "\n\nFull text: [the materials page](materials.html#mismatches).\n")
```

### Internal identities {#internal-identities}

Checks against things that are not inputs to anything:

```{r}
#| label: identities
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "internal consistency checks"
x10 <- t10 %>% left_join(t9 %>% select(scenario, r, WT, C), by = c("scenario", "r", "WT", "C"))
npv_at_breakeven <- with(x10, WT - break_even_pct * C / r)
s_cell <- site_grid_cell(grid, as.list(site_named()$ssrn))
n_cell <- site_grid_cell(grid, as.list(site_named()$nber))
se_s <- mcs$summary$sd / sqrt(mcs$summary$n); se_n <- mcn$summary$sd / sqrt(mcn$summary$n)
checks <- data.frame(
  identity = c(
    "Table 10's x* plugged into Table 9's formula gives NPV = 0 (max |NPV|, $B)",
    "Grid's SSRN cell equals the pipeline's analytic mean (abs diff, $B)",
    "Grid's NBER cell equals the pipeline's analytic mean (abs diff, $B)",
    "SSRN seeded MC mean vs exact expectation, in MC standard errors",
    "NBER seeded MC mean vs exact expectation, in MC standard errors",
    "SSRN share negative: quadrature vs seeded MC (points)",
    "NBER share negative: quadrature vs seeded MC (points)",
    "NBER ceiling: domestic total minus the 7 departures, recomputed minus the script's 72 ($B)"),
  value = c(max(abs(npv_at_breakeven)),
    abs(s_cell$mean_npv - tr("npv_mc_ssrn_analytic_mean")),
    abs(n_cell$mean_npv - tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean")),
    (mcs$summary$mean - tr("npv_mc_ssrn_analytic_mean")) / se_s,
    (mcn$summary$mean - tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean")) / se_n,
    s_cell$pct_negative - mcs$summary$pct_negative,
    n_cell$pct_negative - mcn$summary$pct_negative,
    nc$ceiling_recomputed - nb$wt_max))
checks$value <- vapply(checks$value, function(v) format(signif(v, 3)), "")
scroll(kable(checks))
```

Both seeded means sit within about one Monte Carlo standard error of the exact expectation, on
opposite sides, which is why the SSRN printed mean matches the expectation while the NBER printed
mean matches the seeded run.

## Reproducing this document

```sh
cd rjkdc-analysis
export RAUH_REPO_DIR=/path/to/wealth_tax     # clone of github.com/bjaros20/wealth_tax at 25e84dd
Rscript -e 'targets::tar_make()'             # writes the targets store, export/r/, site/data/, site/explorer/grid.js
Rscript tests/testthat.R                     # full suite
quarto render site/repro.qmd
```

The authors' repository is MIT licensed but not redistributed here; the tests that re-run the
authors' own scripts skip cleanly without it, and the rest of the suite does not need it.
